intro: Lancashire’s only city: Victorian civic grandeur, riverside parks and an easy hub for the Lakes and the coast.
areas: The main shopping street, Winckley Square and the Flag Market.
Victorian riverside parks on the Ribble.
Bars and independent shops close to the university.
sights: Landmark museum and gallery on the Flag Market (check current opening after its refurbishment).
Ornamental gardens, a Japanese garden and river walks.
Traditional market under a restored Victorian canopy.
Home of Preston North End, one of the Football League’s founding clubs.
eat: The county’s slow-baked lamb and potato classic.
arrive: Preston station is on the West Coast Main Line with direct trains to London, Manchester, Glasgow and Blackpool. Manchester Airport is about an hour by train.
around: The centre is walkable; Preston Bus and Stagecoach cover the city and county.
pass: Bus day tickets are available from the operators; check current fares.
when: Spring to early autumn for parks; the Preston Guild is held every 20 years.
tip: Use Preston as a base for Blackpool, the Ribble Valley and the Lake District.

intro: A walled Roman city with medieval Rows, a riverside racecourse and one of the UK’s most popular zoos.
areas: Two-tier medieval galleries of shops around the Cross.
Walk Britain’s most complete Roman and medieval city walls.
Riverside promenade, boat trips and the Queen’s Park Bridge.
sights: Victorian clock on the city walls, one of England’s most photographed.
Medieval cathedral with a rooftop tour.
Remains of Britain’s largest known Roman amphitheatre.
Large conservation zoo a short bus ride north of the city.
The Roodee, claimed as England’s oldest racecourse still in use.
eat: Food hall with local and global stalls.
Restaurants and wine bars in historic buildings.
One of Britain’s oldest named cheeses.
night: Theatre, cinema and library in a converted Odeon.
arrive: Chester station has trains from London, Manchester and North Wales. Liverpool and Manchester airports are under an hour away.
around: The centre is compact and walkable; buses and Park & Ride serve the zoo and suburbs.
pass: Park & Ride and Stagecoach day tickets are available; check current fares.
when: Spring to autumn; race days (May–September) are busy and fun.
tip: Walk the full circuit of the walls, around two miles, for the best introduction to the city.

intro: A historic port city of medieval walls, cruise ships and Titanic stories, with the New Forest close by.
areas: Medieval walls, the Bargate and Tudor House.
Marina, bars and the cruise terminals.
Bars, restaurants and nightlife north of the centre.
sights: Southampton’s maritime story, including the Titanic crew.
Historic house museum in the Old Town.
Some of England’s most complete town walls.
National park with ponies and villages a short drive west.
eat: A cluster of restaurants near Ocean Village.
Leisure dining terrace above the shopping centre.
From the Solent and south coast.
night: One of the largest theatres in the south.
arrive: Southampton Airport has its own rail station (Southampton Airport Parkway). Southampton Central has fast trains to London Waterloo. Red Funnel ferries sail to the Isle of Wight.
around: Bluestar, Unilink and First buses cover the city; the centre is walkable.
pass: Bus day tickets are available from the operators; check current fares.
when: May–September for waterfront events and New Forest days out.
tip: Check the cruise calendar: big ship days fill hotels and taxis.

intro: Britain’s island city and home of the Royal Navy, with a historic dockyard, a seafront and the Spinnaker Tower.
areas: Naval history, waterfront shopping and restaurants.
Cobbled streets, the Round Tower and harbour views.
Seafront, Southsea Castle and Albert Road’s bars.
sights: HMS Victory, the Mary Rose and HMS Warrior.
Viewing tower with a glass floor over the harbour.
Henry VIII’s fort on the seafront.
eat: Fish and chips on the seafront
night: Bars and live music, including The Wedgewood Rooms.
Bars and late venues by the harbour.
arrive: Portsmouth Harbour and Portsmouth & Southsea stations have trains from London Waterloo. Southampton Airport is about 40 minutes away. Wightlink and Hovertravel cross to the Isle of Wight.
around: First and Stagecoach buses cover the city; the seafront is great for walking and cycling.
pass: Bus day tickets are available from the operators; check current fares.
when: May–September; Victorious Festival in late August.
tip: Buy a multi-attraction Dockyard ticket if you plan to see several ships.

intro: A diverse, food-loving city where King Richard III was rediscovered and Diwali lights up the Golden Mile.
areas: Curve theatre, Phoenix cinema and the LCB Depot.
Cathedral, Guildhall and the King Richard III centre.
Indian restaurants, sweet shops and sari stores.
sights: The story of the king found under a car park.
Where Richard III was reburied in 2015.
eat: Belgrave Road’s vegetarian and South Asian restaurants and sweet shops.
One of England’s largest outdoor covered markets.
night: Major theatre in the Cultural Quarter.
One of the largest outside India, in October or November.
arrive: East Midlands Airport is linked by Skylink bus. Leicester station has fast trains to London St Pancras.
around: The centre is walkable; Arriva, First and Centrebus routes cover the city.
pass: Bus day tickets are available from the operators; check current fares.
when: Spring to autumn; Diwali (October or November) and Caribbean Carnival (August).
tip: Arrive hungry on the Golden Mile and try mithai from a sweet shop.

intro: A compact cathedral city at the start of the Derwent Valley Mills World Heritage Site, with the Peak District close by.
areas: Independent shops, bars and restaurants around the cathedral.
The Derwent and the Museum of Making.
Georgian street with bars and restaurants.
sights: In the Silk Mill, part of the Derwent Valley Mills World Heritage Site.
Tallest tower in the city, famous for nesting peregrine falcons.
Paintings by Joseph Wright of Derby.
World Heritage mills north of the city, including Belper and Cromford.
eat: Made in nearby Bakewell in the Peak District.
night: Derby is known for traditional pubs and beer festivals.
arrive: East Midlands Airport is about 30 minutes away. Derby station has direct trains to London St Pancras, Birmingham and Sheffield.
around: Walkable centre; Arriva and trentbarton buses cover the city and the Peak District.
pass: Bus day tickets are available from the operators; check current fares.
when: Spring to autumn for Peak District trips.
tip: Combine a city visit with the Derwent Valley Mills and Matlock Bath.

intro: A city of reinvention: a bombed cathedral beside its modern successor, motor heritage and 2 Tone music.
areas: The cathedrals, the Herbert and medieval streets.
Creative village of independent shops and street food.
Historic street of bars and restaurants.
sights: The bombed medieval ruins and Basil Spence’s 1962 cathedral.
Free museum of cars, bikes and land-speed record vehicles.
Free art and local history museum.
In Broadgate, with the city’s famous legend.
night: The city that gave the world The Specials.
arrive: Birmingham Airport is about 15 minutes by train. Coventry station has fast trains to London Euston and Birmingham.
around: Walkable centre; National Express Coventry and Stagecoach buses cover the city.
pass: West Midlands network day tickets and contactless caps apply on many buses; check current fares.
when: Spring to autumn for outdoor events.
tip: Visit the cathedral ruins at dusk, when the bombed walls are at their most moving.

intro: A Black Country city with a famous football club, fine Victorian art and easy tram links to Birmingham.
areas: Queen Square, Lichfield Street and the Mander Centre.
sights: Victorian art and pop art in the city centre.
Home of Wolves, with stadium tours.
National Trust Arts and Crafts house.
eat: Wolverhampton has a large Sikh and Punjabi community.
arrive: Birmingham Airport is about 40 minutes away. Wolverhampton station has direct trains to London, Birmingham and Manchester.
around: West Midlands Metro trams run to Birmingham; buses cover the city.
pass: West Midlands network tickets and contactless caps cover trams and many buses.
when: Spring to autumn; check the Wolves fixture list.
tip: Ride the tram through the Black Country to Birmingham city centre.

intro: A leafy town between Birmingham and the countryside, home to the NEC, Birmingham Airport and Touchwood.
areas: Touchwood, the High Street and St Alphege Church.
Exhibition halls, arena and leisure complex.
Village high streets with pubs and restaurants.
sights: National Exhibition Centre and bp pulse LIVE arena.
Shopping, dining and entertainment by the NEC.
Parks next to the town centre.
Medieval parish church in the old centre.
eat: Restaurant terrace in the shopping centre.
arrive: Birmingham Airport and Birmingham International station sit within the borough. Solihull station has trains to Birmingham Moor Street and London Marylebone.
around: National Express buses and local trains; many visitors drive.
pass: West Midlands network tickets and contactless caps cover many buses.
when: Year-round; check the NEC events calendar, as big shows fill hotels.
tip: For NEC events, book hotels early or stay in Birmingham and take the train.

intro: The Potteries: six towns made famous by Wedgwood, Spode and Moorcroft, with factory shops and museums.
areas: City centre with the Potteries Museum, theatres and shopping.
Mother town of the Potteries, with Middleport Pottery nearby.
Gladstone Pottery Museum and factory shops.
sights: The last complete Victorian pottery with bottle ovens.
Factory, museum and tearoom at Barlaston.
Gardens, lake, shopping village and Monkey Forest.
eat: Local savoury pancakes from oatcake shops.
Afternoon tea at the pottery visitor centres.
night: Concerts and touring shows in Hanley.
arrive: Stoke-on-Trent station has direct trains to London Euston and Manchester. Manchester Airport is about 45 minutes away.
around: First buses connect the six towns; driving helps for factory shops.
pass: First day tickets are available; check current fares.
when: Spring to autumn; Alton Towers and Trentham are busiest in summer.
tip: Factory shops sell seconds and samples; check opening days before you travel.

intro: A planned new city of parks, lakes and public art, with Bletchley Park’s codebreaking story on its doorstep.
areas: centre:mk, the Theatre District and Campbell Park.
Bletchley Park and the National Museum of Computing.
Willen Lake and the Peace Pagoda.
sights: Home of the Second World War codebreakers.
Working historic computers at Bletchley Park.
Watersports, walks and the Peace Pagoda.
eat: Older town high streets with pubs.
night: Indoor real-snow slope, cinema and bars.
arrive: Milton Keynes Central has fast trains to London Euston and Birmingham. Luton Airport is around 30–40 minutes by road.
around: Buses and Redways (a city-wide network of cycle and walking paths); grid roads make driving easy.
pass: Bus day tickets are available; MK Connect offers on-demand rides.
when: Spring to autumn for the parks and lakes.
tip: Borrow a bike or e-scooter where available and use the Redways.

intro: England’s shoemaking capital, with a historic round church, a Mackintosh house and Saints rugby.
areas: Market Square, the Guildhall and the Cultural Quarter.
sights: Home to a world-famous shoe collection.
House remodelled by Charles Rennie Mackintosh.
One of England’s few surviving medieval round churches.
eat: Market stalls in one of England’s largest market squares.
arrive: Northampton station has trains to London Euston and Birmingham. Luton and Birmingham airports are around an hour away.
around: Stagecoach buses cover the town; the centre is walkable.
pass: Stagecoach day tickets are available; check current fares.
when: Spring to autumn; Silverstone race weekends fill hotels across the county.
tip: Visit the factory shops of famous Northamptonshire shoemakers (check opening hours).

intro: A cathedral city on the River Nene, with the Nene Park lakes and grand Burghley House close by.
areas: Lakes, walking and cycling on the edge of the city.
sights: Norman cathedral where Catherine of Aragon is buried.
Country park with lakes and trails.
arrive: Peterborough station is on the East Coast Main Line, about 45–50 minutes from London King’s Cross. Stansted is about an hour away.
around: Stagecoach buses cover the city; Nene Park is good by bike.
pass: Stagecoach day tickets are available; check current fares.
when: Spring to autumn for the parks and river.
tip: Combine a visit with Stamford, one of England’s best-preserved stone towns.

intro: A historic university city of colleges, chapels, punts on the Cam and riverside meadows.
areas: King’s Parade, Market Square and the colleges.
Riverside lawns behind the colleges, best seen from a punt.
sights: Gothic chapel with a famous fan-vaulted ceiling.
Hire a punt or take a chauffeured trip along the Backs.
Free museum of art and antiquities.
Village reached by a riverside walk.
eat: Associated with the old Fitzbillies bakery.
night: Including The Eagle, where the DNA discovery was announced.
arrive: Cambridge station has trains to London King’s Cross and Liverpool Street, and direct trains to Stansted Airport.
around: Walk or cycle; the centre has limited car access. Buses and Park & Ride run from the outskirts.
pass: Stagecoach day tickets and Park & Ride tickets are available; check current fares.
when: April–June for punting and gardens; avoid exam time if you want college access.
tip: Many colleges charge entry or close at exam times; check before you go.

intro: The city of dreaming spires: golden-stone colleges, world-famous libraries and museums, and punts on the Cherwell.
areas: Radcliffe Camera, Bodleian Library and the High Street.
Multicultural food and nightlife east of the centre.
sights: Guided tours of the historic library buildings.
Free museum of art and archaeology.
College, cathedral and the Great Hall.
Free museums in one striking building.
eat: Historic market with food stalls and cafés.
Restaurants and pubs by the canal.
night: The Turf Tavern and The Bear are among the oldest.
arrive: Oxford station has trains to London Paddington and Marylebone. Airline coaches run to Heathrow and Gatwick, and coaches run frequently to London.
around: Walk the centre; buses and Park & Ride cover the rest. Cycling is popular.
pass: Bus day tickets and Park & Ride options are available; check current fares.
when: Spring and early summer; autumn is lovely as term starts.
tip: Some colleges charge entry and close for events; check visiting hours.

intro: A Thames Valley town with abbey ruins, the Thames and Kennet, and one of Britain’s best-known music festivals.
areas: Broad Street, The Oracle and the riverside.
Reading Abbey ruins and Forbury Gardens.
sights: Founded by Henry I, who is buried there.
Victorian park with the Maiwand Lion.
Includes a full-size Victorian replica of the Bayeux Tapestry.
night: Big rock and pop festival every August bank holiday weekend.
arrive: Reading station has fast trains to London Paddington and the Elizabeth line. RailAir coaches link to Heathrow.
around: Reading Buses cover the town; the centre is walkable.
pass: Reading Buses day tickets and contactless capping; check current fares.
when: Spring to autumn; August bank holiday for the festival.
tip: Book hotels early for the Reading Festival weekend.

intro: A medieval city of cathedral spires, cobbled lanes and a giant market, close to the Norfolk Broads.
areas: One of England’s best-preserved medieval streets.
sights: Norman cathedral with a tall spire and large cloisters.
One of England’s largest open-air markets.
Waterways for boat trips, a short trip away.
arrive: Norwich Airport has limited routes; Norwich station has trains to London Liverpool Street (about two hours).
around: Walkable centre; First and Konect buses serve the city.
pass: Bus day tickets are available; check current fares.
when: May–September for the Broads and outdoor events.
tip: Hire a day boat on the Broads from nearby Wroxham.

intro: Britain’s first recorded town, with Roman walls, a Norman castle and a popular zoo.
areas: High Street, the Dutch Quarter and Castle Park.
Parkland around the castle with Roman remains.
Oysters and beaches south of the city.
sights: The largest surviving Norman keep, built on a Roman temple.
Britain’s oldest surviving Roman town wall.
Large zoo on the edge of the city.
eat: From the nearby Colne estuary and Mersea.
night: Gigs and comedy in a converted church.
arrive: Colchester station has trains to London Liverpool Street (around an hour). Stansted Airport is about 45 minutes by road.
around: Walkable centre; First and Arriva buses serve the area.
pass: Bus day tickets are available; check current fares.
when: Spring to autumn.
tip: Walk the circuit of the Roman wall to see the Balkerne Gate.

intro: Essex’s county town and one of England’s newest cities, the birthplace of radio manufacturing.
areas: High Street, Bond Street and the Cathedral.
sights: Medieval church that became a cathedral in 1914.
Restored Georgian house in landscaped grounds.
Site of the world’s first radio factory.
arrive: Chelmsford station has trains to London Liverpool Street (around 35 minutes). Stansted Airport is about 30 minutes by road.
around: First buses and Park & Ride; the centre is walkable.
pass: Park & Ride and bus day tickets are available; check current fares.
when: Spring to autumn.
tip: Hylands Park hosts big summer events; check dates before booking.

intro: Seaside city at the Thames Estuary, with the world’s longest pleasure pier and Old Leigh’s cockle sheds.
areas: Fishing village with cockle sheds and pubs.
sights: The longest pleasure pier in the world, with its own railway.
arrive: London Southend Airport has its own station. c2c trains run to London Fenchurch Street and Greater Anglia to Liverpool Street.
around: Arriva and First buses; the seafront is good for walking.
pass: Bus day tickets are available; check current fares.
when: May–September for the beach.
tip: Take the pier train out and walk back to see the estuary.
